Logistic Regression: Weighted sum of features (log-odds) passed through a sigmoid to give p(dropout).
Decision Tree: Repeated yes/no questions on one feature at a time; each leaf gives a class and a proportion.
Random Forest: Many decorrelated trees, each trained on a bootstrap sample with random feature subsets; probabilities are averaged.

Logistic Regression: High: one coefficient per feature; odds ratios (per 1 SD after scaling).
Decision Tree: High when shallow: the rule path can be read; falls fast as depth grows.
Random Forest: Low to medium: only importance scores, partial dependence or permutation importance; no single rule path.

Logistic Regression: Low unless transformations or interaction terms (e.g. F21 steps x time) are added by hand.
Decision Tree: High: thresholds and interactions arise from the splits.
Random Forest: High: averages many nonlinear trees; interactions are automatic.

Logistic Regression: Low to medium; controlled with L2 regularisation (C). Can underfit if the true pattern is nonlinear.
Decision Tree: High if deep and unpruned; control with max_depth, min_samples_leaf, ccp_alpha.
Random Forest: Medium: averaging cuts variance, but very deep trees on tiny data can still memorise; check with out-of-bag and CV scores.

Logistic Regression: Low: convex optimisation, fast even on thousands of rows.
Decision Tree: Low: roughly O(p n log n) to build; very fast prediction.
Random Forest: Medium: about n_estimators times one tree; trivial for hundreds of rows, heavier for very large data.

Logistic Regression: Works with small samples if features are few; rule of thumb of about 10 events per candidate parameter (Peduzzi et al., 1996) is a guide, not a law.
Decision Tree: Needs enough rows per leaf; very unstable on small samples (a few rows can change the tree).
Random Forest: Needs more data than LR to show a benefit; with a small survey it may add noise rather than accuracy.

Logistic Regression: Scaling needed (regularisation and solver); one-hot encoding; imputation; watch collinear features.
Decision Tree: No scaling; imputation (or native NaN support in recent scikit-learn); one-hot or ordinal encoding.
Random Forest: No scaling; imputation; one-hot encoding; many-category variables can bias impurity importance.

Logistic Regression: class_weight='balanced'; threshold tuning; report PR-AUC and recall; probabilities are shifted by reweighting, so recalibrate if probabilities are used.
Decision Tree: class_weight='balanced'; min_samples_leaf prevents leaves with no minority cases; threshold tuning.
Random Forest: class_weight='balanced_subsample'; stratified bootstrap options; threshold tuning; PR-AUC.

Logistic Regression: Transparent; gives calibrated-style probabilities; strong baseline; coefficients map directly to hypotheses H1 to H5.
Decision Tree: Readable rules a business team can discuss; finds thresholds (e.g. 'more than 7 steps'); no scaling.
Random Forest: Strong default for tabular data; handles nonlinearity, interactions and mixed feature types; OOB estimate; robust to noise.

Logistic Regression: Misses interactions and curves unless added; sensitive to outliers and collinearity; linear in the log-odds.
Decision Tree: Unstable (high variance); axis-aligned splits only; greedy splitting; probabilities are coarse.
Random Forest: Hard to explain; importance can mislead with correlated or high-cardinality features; larger and slower than the others.

Logistic Regression: Best first model: simple, explainable, matches the hypothesis-driven design and small-data reality.
Decision Tree: Useful second model to look for friction thresholds and to explain patterns to non-technical readers.
Random Forest: Useful third model to test whether nonlinear structure exists; recommended only if it beats LR under the same validation.
